raw_text:
Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were developed to address perceived limitations of permanent metallic drug-eluting stents (DES): chronic caging of the artery, impaired vasomotion, late inflammation, difficulties with future bypass grafting, and a persistent substrate for very late thrombosis. The concept is not new; early poly-L-lactic acid devices demonstrated feasibility but also the challenges of recoil, thick struts, and thrombogenicity [1]. The Absorb everolimus-eluting scaffold became the dominant platform and generated the largest clinical evidence base, beginning with small first-in-human studies that showed acceptable early safety and progressive resorption with partial restoration of vasomotor function [2,3].

The theoretical appeal of BVS rests on three phases: initial mechanical scaffolding and drug delivery, bioresorption with loss of radial strength, and late vascular “uncaging.” Imaging studies from ABSORB cohorts documented late lumen enlargement, plaque sealing, and restoration of some vasoreactivity after scaffold disappearance [4-6]. However, these potential benefits required a device with substantially thicker struts than contemporary cobalt-chromium or platinum-chromium DES, lower acute radial strength, and more demanding implantation technique. These engineering trade-offs proved clinically important.

Randomized trials initially suggested non-inferiority in selected, relatively simple lesions. In ABSORB II, one-year outcomes appeared broadly comparable between Absorb and an everolimus-eluting metallic stent, but by three years the scaffold failed to demonstrate superior vasomotion and had more target-vessel myocardial infarction and device thrombosis [7,8]. ABSORB III similarly met its one-year non-inferiority end point in low-to-moderate complexity lesions, yet later follow-up revealed excess target lesion failure and scaffold thrombosis, particularly in small vessels [9,10]. ABSORB IV incorporated improved patient and lesion selection and emphasized predilatation, appropriate sizing, and post-dilatation; early outcomes improved but did not establish a durable advantage over metallic DES [11].

Regional randomized trials reinforced this mixed picture. ABSORB Japan and ABSORB China confirmed reasonable short-term efficacy in selected lesions but were not powered to detect uncommon late thrombotic events [12,13]. In contrast, AIDA, a pragmatic all-comers trial, found significantly more device thrombosis with Absorb than with a contemporary everolimus-eluting stent, prompting safety concerns and changes in clinical practice [14]. In ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction, TROFI II suggested acceptable early healing by optical coherence tomography, but the broader concern remained that thrombus-rich lesions, malapposition, and undersizing could magnify scaffold risk [15].

Mechanistic studies clarified why outcomes diverged from expectations. Scaffold thrombosis was associated with underexpansion, malapposition, edge dissection, overlap, small reference diameter, discontinuity during resorption, and late dismantling [16-19]. The “PSP” approach—adequate lesion preparation, correct vessel sizing, and high-pressure post-dilatation—was therefore promoted and appears to reduce early adverse events, although it cannot fully eliminate risks related to thick struts and bioresorption biology [20]. These findings shifted BVS from a “stent-like” therapy to a procedure requiring careful lesion selection and meticulous intravascular imaging-guided optimization.

Meta-analyses synthesized the signal: compared with contemporary everolimus-eluting metallic stents, Absorb was associated with higher device thrombosis and target lesion failure, especially beyond the first year and in small vessels [21,22]. Large registries such as GHOST-EU showed that real-world use in complex lesions was feasible but accompanied by non-trivial early and late event rates [23]. Studies in acute coronary syndromes and STEMI remained hypothesis-generating rather than definitive [24].

The field has therefore moved beyond the first-generation Absorb platform. Magnesium-based scaffolds offer faster resorption, greater radial strength than polymeric scaffolds, and potentially less chronic inflammatory burden. BIOSOLVE-I and BIOSOLVE-II showed encouraging angiographic and clinical performance for drug-eluting absorbable metal scaffolds, and BIOSOLVE-IV expanded experience in a larger population [25-27]. Other polymeric devices, including novolimus- and sirolimus-eluting scaffolds, have aimed to improve strut thickness, deliverability, radiopacity, and resorption kinetics [28]. Contemporary reviews emphasize that the failure of first-generation BVS should be interpreted as a device-generation problem rather than proof that transient scaffolding is biologically unsound [29,30].

At present, routine BVS implantation in percutaneous coronary intervention cannot be recommended over best-in-class metallic DES. Potential niches remain: young patients with large proximal vessels, lesions where future surgical access or adaptive remodeling is desirable, and settings in which improved next-generation scaffolds can be implanted with imaging guidance and prolonged antiplatelet adherence. The central lesson is that disappearing hardware is not automatically safer hardware. Future success will require thinner struts, predictable degradation, high radial strength during healing, excellent deliverability and visibility, randomized evidence against contemporary ultrathin DES, and disciplined implantation technique. Until then, BVS remain an instructive but cautionary chapter in the evolution of coronary intervention.
